lines.text: Nearly every atom in it is older than the Earth. Older than the Sun, even.
But its carbon, its oxygen, its calcium, didn't exist when the universe began.
So where did it come from?
The young universe made almost nothing but hydrogen and helium.
Until gravity squeezed it into clumps so hot their cores ignited.
Inside, hydrogen fuses into helium, and that makes light.
Big stars go further. Helium becomes carbon and oxygen, then neon, silicon, and finally, iron.
But iron is a dead end. Fusing it costs energy instead of releasing it.
The core collapses in less than a second,
A supernova, flinging fresh elements into space.
The dust mixes with fresh gas and gathers into new stars and planets.
Four and a half billion years ago, one such cloud became the Sun, the Earth, and eventually, you.
The calcium in your bones, the iron in your blood, the oxygen you breathe, all forged in stars that died before the Sun was born.
You don't just live in the universe. You're made of it.
Old stardust, wondering where it came from.
